Let the room play for a second. "This is your pub, on your own TVs. Every commercial break becomes a Patsy's ad: your tacos, your happy hour, your Thanksgiving Eve party. It costs you nothing in ad money, and we only touch the TVs."
Walk the five lines, then let the spot play. "That's what your guests see during a commercial: your happy hour, your prices, your shamrock. Not someone else's ad."

"Here's a real game. When it goes to commercial, the network ad is gone and your spots play: Taco Tuesday, happy hour, football Sundays. When the game comes back, so do your TVs." Anything technical, say I'll get you the answer.

The box is the SBX-1. Point at the three TVs: real games on every screen, then the break hits and every TV shows a Patsy's spot, and halfway through the break they rotate to the next ones. Keep it simple: "It watches the broadcast. When the game goes to commercial, your TVs show your stuff. When the game comes back, so do your TVs." If they ask how it knows it's a commercial: "That's our patent-pending part. It watches the broadcast, not the room." Don't go deeper than that.

Ask: "What's your best server's best day look like? Every table hears the special, every round gets upsold. That's what this does on every TV, every break." Then: "And it's the lowest-cost employee you'll ever have."
This is straight off their website and menus. Ask if anything changed. Happy hour: the happy hour menu on their site says 3 to 6 daily. Confirm that with the owner.

The bar side. The fall cocktail menu runs through November 26, so that spot comes down on the 27th and the holiday spots go up.

The nights that fill the room. Live music leads: the fiddle and the band are their own stage, on their own TVs. The private party spot is the one that can pay for a whole month: partial pub up to 75, whole pub up to 150.
These are the events already on their website. Each one gets its own spot, running on the TVs for the two weeks before. The owner picks which ones to push.

St. Patrick's is their Super Bowl: three days, March 15 to 17. Starting the TV spots in late February is how you fill three days, not just one. The band spot runs, then the fiddle: their own live music, on their own TVs.

Point at the TV. "The game never leaves the screen. It slides into the corner and trivia runs around it. Guests scan the code and play on their own phones, table against table." Trivia gives a table a reason to stay for one more round. Music is their call: spots run silent, or over royalty-free music in the genre they pick. If they ask about music licensing, say I'll get you that in writing. Never say unlicensed.

Two modes for when there's no game. Loop mode: any TV runs a nonstop loop of their own spots. Good before the first game, or on the TV nobody's watching. After Hours: when the last game ends and nothing's on, flip to our channel of short, funny clips. People keep looking up at the TVs, and their Patsy's spots still play between clips.
This is how the owner knows it worked, from their own numbers: the item sales report their register already prints, plus one question from the staff.

The Founding 10 offer. Never quote a price or a range: pricing isn't set, and the founding venues help set it. If they ask, say the founding-member rate is something we set together after the 90 days, with no obligation to continue.
Close on the asks: their list of about six items and events, the item sales reports, and the staff tally. Then book the install.
